title: The Lives of Others
full_review:
"The Lives of Others" (Sony Classics) is a gripping German political thriller set in East Berlin in 1984, five years before the fall of the Berlin Wall.

Gerd Weisler (Ulrich Muhe), a quietly ruthless interrogator for the secret police (i.e., the Stasi, with an enormous network of 200,000 informants whose job it was to learn everything possible about "the lives of others"), is assigned to wiretap the apartment of celebrated playwright Georg Dreyman (Sebastian Koch), seemingly an upstanding Communist Party member, and his actress companion, Christa-Maria Sieland (Martina Gedeck).

The order has come from Minister Bruno Hempf (Thomas Thieme), via Weisler's friend Lt. Col. Anton Grubitz (Ulrich Tukur), head of the Culture Department. Hempf's motives have little to do with official party concerns, but rather, he has taken a romantic interest in Sieland, and would like nothing more than for Dreyman to be out of the way.

Pressured into commencing a sordid affair with Hempf, Sieland is plagued with guilt but feels she must continue the clandestine trysts with him or else. (Adding to her vulnerability is her secret drug addiction.)

Weisler takes on the assignment with his usual cold efficiency, but lo and behold, something wondrous happens. As he assiduously eavesdrops on the couple and their artistic friends -- including once-prominent theater director Albert Jerska (Volkmar Kleinert), now tragically blacklisted by the government -- Weisler begins to discover his own humanity in the process.

Without revealing what happens next, the stage is set for a most compelling and thought-provoking resolution.

Writer-director Florian Henckel von Donnersmarck, making an auspicious feature film debut, has crafted a profoundly moving story that besides bringing to life the ambience of pre-glasnost Germany, vividly demonstrates the transformative power of art, while elucidating the conflict between ideology and conscience.

The performances, especially that of Muhe, are superb.

Quite simply, this is a modern classic, fully deserving the awards and accolades it has already garnered in Europe.

Subtitles.

The film contains some sexual encounters, one involving a prostitute, with rear and partial nudity; a premarital relationship; innuendo; a few crude words; drug addiction; and suicide. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
